subtopic_detail: Immediate manoeuvres for umbilical cord prolapse at full dilation in a term singleton
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar attending a 28 year old woman gravida 2 para 1 in the labour ward at 39 weeks gestation. She has been in the second stage of labour for 20 minutes with the head at station +1 and ruptured membranes 45 minutes ago. Immediately after a spontaneous surge of amniotic fluid the midwife notes a loop of pulsating cord in the vagina. Cardiotocograph shows immediate profound decelerations to 60 /min lasting more than 2 minutes. She has no known allergies. She has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth 2 years ago at term.

Epidural is in situ and functional. Theatre has been alerted. Anaesthetics have been called. Blood is available on standby. The paediatric team is on the way for resuscitation. She is fully dilated with vertex presentation and no shoulder dystocia risk factors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Fully dilated, vertex station +1, cord palpable in vagina and pulsating, loop of cord visible externally
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph profound deceleration to 60 /min lasting >2 minutes, no bleeding, foetal scalp electrode not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Immediately push the cord back inside the vagina above the presenting part and prepare for a planned category 1 caesarean section
options.rationale: Manual replacement of the cord above the presenting part is not recommended because of vasospasm risk and unreliable outcome; manual elevation of the presenting part and appropriate positioning is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline

options.text: Elevate the presenting part with a gloved hand and adopt knee to chest position, plan immediate assisted vaginal delivery if feasible
options.rationale: Immediate manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand plus a knee to chest (or exaggerated Sim) position relieves cord compression while the plan is enacted. If she is fully dilated with a vertex at station +1 in an experienced obstetrician's hands, an assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) is faster than a caesarean and is the recommended mode. Otherwise, urgent category 1 caesarean is performed. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline

options.text: Wrap the cord in warmed saline soaked gauze and delay urgent delivery pending intrapartum ultrasound assessment of the foetal heart
options.rationale: Keeping the cord moist is a supportive measure but does not replace urgent delivery; delay to await ultrasound is inappropriate given the profound deceleration. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline

options.text: Instruct the woman to actively push with contractions in the left lateral position to expedite vaginal delivery of the foetal head
options.rationale: Active pushing may increase cord compression; the aim is to relieve pressure on the cord and deliver rapidly by the fastest safe mode. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline

options.text: Insert a Foley catheter and fill the bladder with 500 mL saline as the sole immediate manoeuvre before proceeding to theatre now
options.rationale: Bladder filling with 500 mL saline lifts the presenting part off the cord as a bridging measure specifically when transfer to theatre is expected to be prolonged; it is not the sole immediate action and manual elevation of the presenting part is faster. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is a category 1 obstetric emergency. Immediate manoeuvres are manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord, positioning the woman knee to chest or exaggerated Sim to relieve cord compression, and calling for urgent delivery. If she is fully dilated with a vertex at low station in an experienced obstetrician's hands, an assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) is the fastest mode; otherwise category 1 caesarean is performed. Bladder filling with 500 mL saline is a bridging technique if transfer to theatre is expected to be delayed (rural or prolonged transport), and tocolysis with terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneous may be considered if uterine relaxation is needed as a bridging step. Keep the cord warm and moist and avoid excess handling.
key_points: Manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord plus knee to chest position is the immediate action.
Fastest safe mode: assisted vaginal delivery at low station full dilation, otherwise category 1 caesarean.
Bladder filling 500 mL is a bridging technique if delivery is delayed.
explanation.pearls: Cord prolapse at full dilation with vertex at +1: manual elevation of the presenting part plus knee to chest position, then assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps) as the fastest safe mode; category 1 caesarean if delivery is not immediately feasible.

sources.label: RANZCOG Intrapartum Care Guideline
Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists Green Top Guideline on Umbilical Cord Prolapse

subtopic_detail: Discriminating asymptomatic uterine dehiscence from uterine rupture at trial of labour after caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman gravida 2 para 1 with one previous transverse lower segment caesarean 3 years ago. She is undergoing a trial of labour after caesarean at 40 weeks. She has been in labour for 8 hours; the cardiotocograph is reassuring; her contractions are 4 in 10, moderate to strong. She is 8 cm dilated with a well applied vertex at station 0. She reports mild suprapubic discomfort persistent between contractions but is otherwise well. She has an epidural in situ providing effective analgesia. Vaginal blood loss is normal.

A bedside ultrasound performed for parental reassurance shows the lower segment scar with an area of thinning (2 mm) but continuous serosa overlying it. There is no free fluid. Foetal heart tracing is category I. Blood pressure and pulse are stable. She has no shoulder pain. She has no gross haematuria on urinary catheter.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus contracting regularly, cervix 8 cm dilated vertex station 0, no vaginal bleeding above normal show, no palpable foetal parts abdominally, uterine tone normal between contractions
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph category I, bedside ultrasound lower segment scar thinned to 2 mm with continuous serosa, no free fluid, urinary catheter clear urine, haemoglobin 116 g/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section for suspected uterine rupture and activation of massive transfusion protocol at this point today
options.rationale: Uterine rupture is defined by disruption of the serosa with foetal or placental parts extruding; findings here are of dehiscence with intact serosa and stable maternal and foetal parameters; category 1 caesarean is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Perform manual palpation of the uterine scar transvaginally under general anaesthetic to assess for continuity before further management
options.rationale: Manual transvaginal palpation is not routine before delivery in trial of labour after caesarean; scar integrity is assessed clinically and by ultrasound. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Give tocolysis with terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously and continue with the trial of labour after caesarean without further review
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not indicated without an abnormal cardiotocograph or evidence of hyperstimulation; it is used to buy time in confirmed foetal distress before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Increase oxytocin augmentation to 8 mU/min to accelerate labour and reduce the total time the scar is exposed to contractions today
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation increases uterine rupture risk in trial of labour after caesarean and requires careful indication and senior obstetric supervision; it is not increased in response to a suspected scar concern. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

options.text: Continue trial of labour after caesarean with continuous cardiotocograph and senior obstetric review; act on evolving features suggesting rupture
options.rationale: Uterine dehiscence with intact serosa on ultrasound, a reassuring cardiotocograph and stable maternal and foetal parameters can continue trial of labour after caesarean with continuous cardiotocograph monitoring and senior obstetric awareness. Uterine rupture is diagnosed clinically by loss of station of the presenting part, acute foetal distress (particularly prolonged deceleration or bradycardia), maternal haemodynamic collapse, vaginal bleeding out of keeping, and severe abdominal pain that persists between contractions. Ultrasound scar thinning alone is not diagnostic. (Source: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture is a clinical diagnosis, not a radiological one. It is characterised by loss of station of the presenting part, acute foetal distress (particularly prolonged deceleration or bradycardia), maternal haemodynamic collapse, vaginal bleeding out of keeping, and severe abdominal pain persisting between contractions. Uterine dehiscence is asymptomatic scar thinning or incomplete disruption with intact serosa and is a not uncommon finding at repeat caesarean; scar thinning alone on ultrasound is not diagnostic of impending rupture and is not an indication for delivery in the absence of clinical features. Trial of labour after caesarean is continued with continuous cardiotocograph and senior obstetric awareness. Rupture is treated with immediate category 1 caesarean and repair.
key_points: Uterine rupture is a clinical diagnosis: loss of station, prolonged deceleration, haemodynamic collapse, severe persistent abdominal pain.
Dehiscence is asymptomatic scar thinning with intact serosa and is not itself an indication for delivery.
Confirmed rupture: immediate category 1 caesarean and repair with senior obstetric involvement.
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound scar thinning with intact serosa and a reassuring cardiotocograph is dehiscence, not rupture: continue trial of labour after caesarean with continuous cardiotocograph and senior obstetric review; rupture is diagnosed clinically by loss of station, prolonged deceleration, maternal collapse or severe persistent abdominal pain.

sources.label: RANZCOG Vaginal Birth After Caesarean Section Guideline
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists Practice Bulletin on Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery

subtopic_detail: Maternal cardiac arrest at 30 weeks requiring perimortem caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar attending a code blue on the medical ward for a 32 year old primigravida at 30 weeks gestation who has collapsed 30 seconds ago. She was admitted 2 days ago with severe pre-eclampsia at 30 weeks. She has been receiving magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour infusion since admission. She is now pulseless. Advanced life support has commenced with high quality chest compressions, ventilation via bag valve mask, and manual left uterine displacement. Adrenaline 1 mg has been given intravenously. An initial rhythm check shows pulseless electrical activity.

The medical emergency team is present. The neonatology team is being called. Theatre is 5 floors away. There is a category 1 caesarean scalpel pack at the bedside. The obstetric consultant is en route from home. She has been in cardiac arrest for approximately 2 minutes now. There is no return of spontaneous circulation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse absent, blood pressure not recordable, respiratory rate assisted by bag valve mask, SpO2 not tracing during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, temperature 37.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Gravid uterus at umbilicus, pulseless electrical activity on cardiac monitor, effective chest compressions ongoing, manual left uterine displacement in progress
data_table.Investigations: Not available in acute resuscitation; magnesium level from earlier today 2.4 mmol/L (therapeutic pre-eclampsia range 2.0-3.5)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next intervention if there is no return of spontaneous circulation?

options.text: Transport her urgently to theatre for caesarean once the theatre team has scrubbed and prepared the sterile equipment on standby
options.rationale: Transport delays perimortem caesarean and worsens both maternal and foetal outcomes; perimortem caesarean is performed at the site of the arrest. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Insert a supraglottic airway and continue advanced life support for a further 5 minutes before proceeding to perimortem caesarean
options.rationale: Definitive airway is a parallel priority in advanced life support but must not delay perimortem caesarean; airway placement is done in parallel with the perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Give a further 1 mg adrenaline and continue advanced life support for 10 minutes before perimortem caesarean is considered
options.rationale: Waiting 10 minutes worsens both maternal and foetal outcomes; the 4 minute rule is a maternal resuscitation intervention, not a foetal one, and is initiated as soon as return of spontaneous circulation is not achieved. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Discontinue magnesium sulfate and administer calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent by intravenous injection now over 3 minutes
options.rationale: Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously is given for suspected magnesium toxicity contributing to arrest but is not the definitive next step above perimortem caesarean; both may be done but the perimortem caesarean is the highest priority action if there is no return of spontaneous circulation. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

options.text: Perform perimortem caesarean at the bedside aiming to deliver by 4 minutes into cardiac arrest, do not transport to theatre
options.rationale: The 4 minute rule states that perimortem caesarean should commence by 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest with a viable foetus at or beyond 20 to 24 weeks (fundus at or above the umbilicus) with delivery by 5 minutes. It is a maternal resuscitation intervention (aortocaval decompression improves cardiac output up to 25 percent) and is performed at the bedside without transport, without full sterility and without waiting for anaesthesia because the mother is arrested. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: The 4 minute rule for perimortem caesarean states that if there is no return of spontaneous circulation by 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest with a viable foetus at or beyond 20 to 24 weeks (uterus at or above the umbilicus), a perimortem caesarean is commenced with delivery by 5 minutes. It is a maternal resuscitation intervention because aortocaval decompression improves cardiac output up to 25 percent. It is performed at the bedside without transport, without full sterility and without waiting for anaesthesia because the mother is arrested. Chest compressions and defibrillation are continued during the procedure and manual left uterine displacement is maintained until the abdomen is opened. Suspected magnesium toxicity is treated with calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously in parallel.
key_points: Perimortem caesarean starts at 4 minutes of arrest, aim delivery by 5 minutes.
Performed at the bedside; do not transport; continue chest compressions.
Suspected magnesium toxicity: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously in parallel.
explanation.pearls: Maternal cardiac arrest at 30 weeks: perimortem caesarean at bedside starting at 4 minutes of arrest with delivery by 5 minutes; continue chest compressions and give calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously in parallel if magnesium toxicity is suspected.

sources.label: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline on Resuscitation in Pregnancy
American Heart Association Scientific Statement on Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion identified antenatally requires multidisciplinary planning
stem:
You are the maternal foetal medicine registrar reviewing a 37 year old woman gravida 4 para 3 at 30 weeks gestation with three previous caesareans. She had an in vitro fertilisation pregnancy. Ultrasound at 20 weeks noted anterior placenta praevia. Magnetic resonance imaging at 28 weeks demonstrated an anterior placenta praevia with loss of the retroplacental clear space, disruption of the bladder wall interface, hypertrophic subplacental vessels, and focal bulging of the placenta into the bladder consistent with placenta percreta with bladder invasion. She has had no vaginal bleeding. She has not received antenatal steroids.

She has been referred to your quaternary obstetric centre. Multidisciplinary review is planned for this week. She is otherwise well. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L; she is on iron replacement. She has no known allergies. Her BMI is 27 kg/m^2. She has a longstanding preference to preserve fertility but is prepared to consider hysterectomy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 30 cm, no palpable bladder, no vaginal blood, no clinical anaemia, no palpable adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging placenta percreta with bladder invasion, ultrasound anterior praevia and lacunar spaces, haemoglobin 108 g/L, group O positive with antibody screen negative

lead_in: Which combination best matches the AU recommended peri-operative plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean at 37+0 weeks by local obstetrician alone with a plan to remove the placenta manually as usual after delivery of the baby
options.rationale: Local single obstetrician management is inadequate for placenta percreta with bladder invasion; multidisciplinary quaternary centre care is essential, and 37+0 does not allow for the increased unplanned delivery risk. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 39+0 weeks with a plan for placental removal, no hysterectomy is planned regardless of intraoperative findings today
options.rationale: 39+0 is too late in placenta accreta spectrum (risk of unplanned labour and antepartum haemorrhage) and attempted placental removal in percreta risks catastrophic haemorrhage; caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 35+6 weeks is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline

options.text: Elective vaginal induction at 39+0 weeks with plan for uterine artery embolisation as needed intra-operatively, no caesarean planned initially
options.rationale: Vaginal induction is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum; caesarean is mandated. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal betamethasone, cell salvage, and planned intraoperative caesarean hysterectomy
options.rationale: In placenta accreta spectrum with high risk features (multiple prior caesareans, in vitro fertilisation pregnancy, bladder invasion), RANZCOG advises planned delivery at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids at a quaternary centre with a placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team, cross matched blood with cell salvage, senior gynaecology surgery, urology on standby for bladder involvement, and planned caesarean hysterectomy leaving the placenta in situ or performing a controlled removal. Fertility preservation is not appropriate given morbidly adherent bladder invasion. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline

options.text: Elective caesarean at 32+0 weeks with immediate hysterectomy regardless of foetal maturity or antenatal corticosteroid course status today
options.rationale: 32+0 imposes significant neonatal prematurity morbidity without a specific clinical trigger; timing is 34+0 to 35+6 with antenatal corticosteroids unless bleeding or preterm labour supervenes. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with high risk features (multiple caesareans, in vitro fertilisation pregnancy, bladder invasion) is delivered at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks at a quaternary centre with a placenta accreta spectrum multidisciplinary team, antenatal corticosteroids, cross matched blood, cell salvage, senior gynaecology surgery, urology on standby, interventional radiology (uterine artery balloon occlusion available), and planned caesarean hysterectomy leaving the placenta in situ or performing controlled removal. Attempted routine placental removal in percreta risks catastrophic haemorrhage. Preoperative counselling includes hysterectomy, transfusion, bladder repair or cystectomy, ureteric injury and intensive care. Fertility preservation is not appropriate in true percreta with organ invasion.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum with bladder invasion: elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids.
Quaternary centre, placenta accreta spectrum team, cell salvage, urology on standby, planned caesarean hysterectomy.
Attempted placental removal in percreta risks catastrophic haemorrhage; leave the placenta in situ or controlled removal.
explanation.pearls: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion: elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with antenatal betamethasone, cell salvage, planned caesarean hysterectomy at a quaternary centre with the placenta accreta spectrum team and urology on standby.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum Guideline
International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics consensus guidelines on placenta accreta spectrum

subtopic_detail: Severe preeclampsia with severe features at 27 weeks: expectant vs immediate delivery
stem:
You are the maternal foetal medicine registrar reviewing a 26 year old primigravida at 27+3 weeks with new severe pre-eclampsia. Blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg despite oral labetalol 200 mg 8 hourly and nifedipine 40 mg 12 hourly. She has proteinuria 4+ on dipstick and a protein creatinine ratio 340 mg/mmol. She has mild frontal headache which resolved with paracetamol. She has no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, no oliguria. Platelets are 148 x10^9/L, liver enzymes normal, creatinine 78 micromol/L, uric acid 0.42 mmol/L. Foetal growth is on the 10th centile, umbilical artery Doppler is normal with a positive end diastolic flow, biophysical profile is 8 of 10, cardiotocograph is category I.

Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis has started. She has received a first dose of betamethasone. She is asking about delivery timing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, symphysis fundal height 26 cm, no epigastric tenderness, no clonus, brisk deep tendon reflexes 3+, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Protein creatinine ratio 340 mg/mmol, platelets 148 x10^9/L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, uric acid 0.42 mmol/L, ultrasound estimated foetal weight 10th centile, umbilical artery Doppler positive end diastolic flow, biophysical profile 8

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Emergency caesarean within 30 minutes as immediate delivery is required for all severe pre-eclampsia regardless of gestational age and current status
options.rationale: Immediate delivery is not mandated in all severe pre-eclampsia at 27 weeks; expectant management under close surveillance improves neonatal outcomes when maternal and foetal conditions are stable and antihypertensive control is achievable. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Change to oral methyldopa 500 mg 6 hourly and manage as an outpatient with weekly clinic review of blood pressure and urinalysis testing
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at 27 weeks with blood pressure 168/112 mmHg requires inpatient management; outpatient management is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Expectant management with close inpatient monitoring, complete steroid course, escalate antihypertensives, deliver at 34 weeks or earlier if criteria trigger
options.rationale: In severe pre-eclampsia at less than 34 weeks with severe hypertension but no persistent uncontrolled hypertension, HELLP syndrome, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, eclampsia, abruption or non reassuring foetal status, expectant management with close inpatient monitoring, complete antenatal steroid course, escalated antihypertensives and delivery at 34 weeks (or earlier if criteria trigger) improves neonatal outcomes. Foetal wellbeing surveillance includes daily cardiotocograph, weekly umbilical artery Doppler and growth every 2 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Induction of labour after prostaglandin ripening within the next 48 hours regardless of foetal weight or cervical status assessment result
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 27 weeks worsens neonatal outcomes when expectant management criteria are met; induction is also inappropriate before completing an antenatal steroid course. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Add aspirin 150 mg daily and discharge home for weekly outpatient blood pressure review and repeat proteinuria testing at general practice
options.rationale: Aspirin is a prevention strategy from before 16 weeks in high risk women, not a treatment for established severe pre-eclampsia; inpatient management is required. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

explanation.summary: In severe pre-eclampsia with severe features at less than 34 weeks, expectant management under close inpatient surveillance with antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and titrated antihypertensives improves neonatal outcomes and is recommended when maternal and foetal conditions are stable. Delivery is triggered by eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, uncontrolled hypertension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, abruption, non reassuring cardiotocograph, absent or reversed umbilical artery end diastolic flow, or gestational age at or beyond 34 weeks. Antihypertensive targets are 140 to 155 mmHg systolic and 90 to 105 mmHg diastolic. Persistent visual disturbance, epigastric pain, headache resistant to simple analgesia and clonus are red flags.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia at <34 weeks: expectant management with steroids, magnesium and antihypertensives when maternal and foetal criteria are met.
Deliver at 34 weeks or earlier for eclampsia, HELLP, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, uncontrolled hypertension, abruption or non reassuring cardiotocograph.
Blood pressure targets: systolic 140 to 155 mmHg and diastolic 90 to 105 mmHg.
explanation.pearls: Severe pre-eclampsia at 27+3 with stable maternal and foetal status: expectant management with steroids, magnesium sulfate, escalated antihypertensives; deliver at 34 weeks or earlier if HELLP, eclampsia, pulmonary oedema, renal failure, abruption or absent umbilical artery end diastolic flow.

sources.label: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline
SOMANZ Guideline for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: High grade squamous vulval intraepithelial neoplasia treatment selection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman with a persistent pruritic vulval lesion at the right labia minora. She was referred with an ill defined 2 cm hyperpigmented plaque with slight thickening but no ulceration or invasion. She has never had cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. She is a current smoker (20 cigarettes/day for 20 years). She has never been vaccinated against human papillomavirus. She is otherwise well. She has no immunosuppression. She wishes to preserve the anatomy of the vulva where safe. She is not planning further pregnancies.

Colposcopy and biopsy under local anaesthetic have returned reporting vulval high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive) with no invasive component. There is no adjacent lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. Examination of the vagina and cervix is normal. No inguinal lymphadenopathy is palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Ill defined 2 cm hyperpigmented plaque with mild thickening right labia minora, no ulceration, no palpable inguinal nodes, vagina and cervix normal
data_table.Investigations: Colposcopy directed biopsy vulval high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive), no invasive component

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Wide local excision with a 5 mm negative peripheral margin as the definitive management strategy for high grade squamous vulval lesions
options.rationale: Wide local excision remains an option and is preferred when occult invasion is suspected, but topical imiquimod is a valid conservative option for unifocal usual type high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion without suspicion of invasion, particularly when anatomy preservation is desired. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline

options.text: Reassurance and clinical review at 12 months without treatment given no evidence of invasion and expectant management is a valid option
options.rationale: High grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion has significant progression risk to invasive cancer; treatment is indicated rather than expectant management. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline

options.text: Vulvectomy (simple total) as a preventative measure to remove all human papillomavirus infected epithelium in this current smoker with HPV 16
options.rationale: Simple vulvectomy is not appropriate for a unifocal high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; it is disfiguring and reserved for extensive multifocal disease or invasion. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline

options.text: External beam radiotherapy 45 Gy in 25 fractions to the vulva and inguinofemoral nodes as first line treatment for high grade lesions
options.rationale: Radiotherapy is reserved for invasive vulval cancer, not vulval intraepithelial neoplasia; it is not first line for high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline

options.text: Topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 16 weeks and re-biopsy any residual lesion; smoking cessation and colposcopy follow up
options.rationale: Topical imiquimod 5 percent applied three times weekly for 12 to 20 weeks (typically 16 weeks) is a first line option for unifocal high grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion of usual type without suspicion of invasion, especially when preservation of anatomy is important. Wide local excision remains an alternative and is preferred when occult invasion is suspected. Smoking cessation reduces recurrence, and post treatment colposcopy at 6 months and then annually is required. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Vulval Intraepithelial Neoplasia Guideline

explanation.summary: Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia of usual type (high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, human papillomavirus related) is most common in premenopausal women and is a precursor for vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Treatment options for unifocal disease without suspicion of invasion are topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 12 to 20 weeks or wide local excision with a 5 mm peripheral margin. Wide local excision is preferred when there is suspicion of occult invasion, at symptomatic thickened or ulcerated lesions, or when compliance with topical therapy is a concern. Smoking cessation reduces recurrence, and follow up colposcopy at 6 months then annually detects recurrence. Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (lichen sclerosus associated) has a higher progression rate and is treated by wide local excision.
key_points: Unifocal high grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion of usual type: topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 12 to 20 weeks or wide local excision with a 5 mm margin.
Wide local excision is preferred when occult invasion is suspected.
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (lichen sclerosus associated) has higher progression risk and is treated by wide local excision.
explanation.pearls: Unifocal high grade squamous vulval intraepithelial lesion (usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive): topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 16 weeks with smoking cessation and colposcopy follow up at 6 months and annually.

European Society of Gynaecological Oncology guidelines for vulval intraepithelial neoplasia

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection for severe behavioural disturbance in dementia with Lewy bodies
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 78 year old man on a general medical ward with fluctuating visual hallucinations, marked cognitive fluctuation and Parkinsonism. He was admitted 3 days ago with a urinary tract infection which has been treated. His hallucinations preceded the infection by 2 months, are typically well formed animals, and his family have noted marked cognitive fluctuation over 8 months alongside dream enactment behaviour and mild bradykinesia. He is now agitated overnight, throwing furniture and threatening staff. He has capacity to consent when lucid, but was assessed 3 hours ago as lacking capacity for treatment decisions. Non pharmacological measures have failed.

His general practitioner previously trialled haloperidol 0.5 mg for a similar episode and he developed severe worsening of Parkinsonism requiring inpatient rehabilitation. He is on rivastigmine 4.6 mg patch daily, ramipril and atorvastatin. He is on no other psychotropic medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor left arm, fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations of animals reported by patient
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, C reactive protein, liver function tests all within normal limits after urinary tract infection treatment; urine culture negative on repeat

lead_in: Which pharmacological approach is most appropriate now?

options.text: Quetiapine 12.5 to 25 mg orally as the initial low dose antipsychotic with close monitoring for extrapyramidal or sedation side effects
options.rationale: In dementia with Lewy bodies, first generation antipsychotics such as haloperidol and higher potency second generation antipsychotics such as risperidone and olanzapine carry a high risk of severe neuroleptic sensitivity reaction. Quetiapine (starting 12.5 to 25 mg oral) and clozapine (specialist supervision) are the preferred antipsychotics if pharmacotherapy is required after non pharmacological measures have failed. Continue cholinesterase inhibitor. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia

options.text: Haloperidol 2.5 mg intramuscular as an initial rapid tranquillisation option because he is already familiar with typical antipsychotics
options.rationale: Haloperidol carries a high risk of severe neuroleptic sensitivity reaction in dementia with Lewy bodies (marked worsening of Parkinsonism, catatonia, malignant syndrome); avoided regardless of prior exposure. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia

options.text: Risperidone 0.5 mg orally as the initial antipsychotic because it is TGA approved for behavioural and psychological symptoms in this population
options.rationale: Risperidone has TGA approval for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia in Alzheimer disease but is high risk in dementia with Lewy bodies because of neuroleptic sensitivity reaction; quetiapine is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg orally wafer as the initial antipsychotic option because he requires rapid onset given the significant agitation risk
options.rationale: Olanzapine has significant anticholinergic burden and D2 blockade risk of worsening Parkinsonism in dementia with Lewy bodies; not preferred. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally as monotherapy for rapid tranquillisation and continue as a scheduled dose regimen at 8 hourly intervals
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines in elderly patients with Lewy body dementia increase confusion, falls and paradoxical agitation risk; not preferred as monotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is characterised by cognitive fluctuation, well formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous Parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder. Severe neuroleptic sensitivity reaction (worsening Parkinsonism, autonomic instability, cognitive worsening, sometimes malignant syndrome) occurs with first generation antipsychotics and with higher potency second generation antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine). Quetiapine 12.5 to 25 mg starting or clozapine (specialist supervision) are the preferred antipsychotics if pharmacotherapy is essential after non pharmacological measures have failed. Continue cholinesterase inhibitor which improves psychosis and cognition in dementia with Lewy bodies. Screen for delirium precipitants (infection, medication, constipation) first.
key_points: Dementia with Lewy bodies is highly sensitive to typical and higher potency second generation antipsychotics.
Preferred pharmacotherapy: quetiapine 12.5 to 25 mg starting or clozapine under specialist supervision.
Continue cholinesterase inhibitor; screen for delirium precipitants first.
explanation.pearls: Severe behavioural disturbance in dementia with Lewy bodies after failed non pharmacological measures: quetiapine 12.5 to 25 mg orally with close monitoring; avoid haloperidol, risperidone and olanzapine.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline on Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia
Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Dementia

subtopic_detail: Discriminating somatic symptom disorder from illness anxiety disorder in a general practice setting
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman who has been on your patient list for 3 years. She has attended the practice on more than 30 occasions over that period with varied somatic complaints (headache, abdominal pain, joint pain, dizziness, fatigue, tingling in fingers) despite repeatedly normal investigation. She experiences significant distress with her symptoms and spends most of her day thinking about her health. She has curtailed her work hours because of the symptoms. She is not preoccupied with a specific illness but is distressed by the symptoms themselves.

Her physical examination is normal and her recent workup (full blood count, urea and electrolytes, C reactive protein, thyroid function, iron studies, magnetic resonance imaging brain, colonoscopy, gastroscopy, echocardiogram, nerve conduction studies) is all within normal limits. She has capacity. She agrees to see you regularly and is open to a mental health discussion. She has no active suicidal ideation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, no focal neurology, no organomegaly, no tenderness on abdominal palpation, mood mildly dysthymic, no psychotic features on brief mental state examination
data_table.Investigations: All prior investigations (full blood count, urea and electrolytes, C reactive protein, thyroid function, iron studies, magnetic resonance imaging brain, colonoscopy, gastroscopy, echocardiogram, nerve conduction studies) within normal limits

lead_in: Which diagnosis best describes her presentation?

options.text: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) because non anatomic sensory symptoms are prominent among her somatic complaints today
options.rationale: Functional neurological disorder requires clear positive neurological signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign, non anatomic sensory loss); her presentation is multi symptom without discrete conversion features. (Source: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline

options.text: Illness anxiety disorder because the essential feature is preoccupation with a specific illness together with a distressing symptom pattern
options.rationale: Illness anxiety disorder features preoccupation with having or acquiring a specific serious illness with minimal or absent somatic symptoms; her presentation is dominated by somatic symptoms, not a specific illness preoccupation. (Source: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder because the emphasis is on multiple somatic symptoms and disproportionate thoughts, feelings and behaviours around them
options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision) is diagnosed when one or more distressing or life disrupting somatic symptoms are accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours related to the symptoms (disproportionate persistent thinking about seriousness, high anxiety about health, excessive time and energy on symptoms). Illness anxiety disorder in contrast has minimal or absent somatic symptoms and preoccupation is with having or acquiring a specific serious illness. (Source: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline

options.text: Malingering because there is no evidence of physical disease despite an extensive workup that included specialist referral over three years
options.rationale: Malingering requires deliberate fabrication of symptoms for external gain; there is no such evidence and she is genuinely distressed. (Source: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline

options.text: Factitious disorder because she has attended more than 30 times with multi system symptoms despite normal investigations over three years
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires deliberate falsification of symptoms without external gain (motivated by the sick role); no such evidence exists in this vignette. (Source: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline

explanation.summary: Somatic symptom disorder in Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision requires one or more distressing or life disrupting somatic symptoms accompanied by disproportionate thoughts, feelings or behaviours (persistent thinking about seriousness, high health anxiety, excessive time and energy on symptoms) for at least 6 months. Illness anxiety disorder in contrast has preoccupation with having or acquiring a specific serious illness with minimal or absent somatic symptoms. Functional neurological disorder requires positive neurological signs of internal inconsistency. Management principles are regular structured review with one nominated general practitioner, minimisation of repeat investigation, treatment of comorbid anxiety and depression, and structured psychological therapy (cognitive behavioural therapy).
key_points: Somatic symptom disorder: distressing symptoms plus disproportionate thoughts, feelings or behaviours for at least 6 months.
Illness anxiety disorder: preoccupation with having or acquiring a specific illness with minimal or absent somatic symptoms.
Management: nominated general practitioner, structured regular review, cognitive behavioural therapy, avoid repeat investigation.
explanation.pearls: Multiple distressing somatic symptoms plus disproportionate health related thoughts and behaviours over more than 6 months without preoccupation with a specific illness is somatic symptom disorder; treat with a nominated general practitioner, structured review and cognitive behavioural therapy.

sources.label: RANZCP Somatic Symptom Disorders Guideline
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision

subtopic_detail: Persistent depressive disorder differentiation from major depressive disorder in general practice
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 34 year old man who says he has felt persistently low mood for most of the day for as long as he can remember, at least the last 4 years. He describes low energy, low self esteem, poor concentration, mild insomnia and mild appetite reduction. There have been no periods of at least 2 weeks free of these symptoms in the last 4 years. He functions at work but says he has never really felt happy. He denies suicidal ideation or intent. He drinks 2 standard drinks per week and does not use illicit substances. He has never had a manic or hypomanic episode.

He has previously been trialled on sertraline 50 mg with no benefit at 8 weeks. He has never had structured psychological therapy. He is not currently on any medication. He has capacity. He is asking about diagnosis and next steps at general practice level.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, dysthymic affect, coherent thought form, no psychomotor slowing, no cognitive impairment, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function, iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate, vitamin D, urine drug screen all within normal limits; Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 14

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits his presentation?

options.text: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood because his depressive symptoms have persisted after an identifiable psychosocial stressor at work
options.rationale: Adjustment disorder occurs within 3 months of an identifiable stressor and resolves within 6 months of its termination; a chronic 4 year course does not fit. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Major depressive disorder single episode because his Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score is 14 which represents moderate depression severity
options.rationale: Major depressive disorder requires a distinct 2 week episode; his symptom pattern is chronic without a distinct episodic pattern and better fits persistent depressive disorder. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cyclothymic disorder because he has chronic mood variability lasting more than 2 years without a full manic or full depressive episode either
options.rationale: Cyclothymic disorder requires alternating subsyndromal hypomanic and depressive symptoms; his presentation is unipolar depression. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder (formerly dysthymia) because low mood is present for at least 2 years without a symptom free interval above 2 months
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision) is diagnosed when depressed mood is present for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults, with at least 2 of poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self esteem, poor concentration and hopelessness, and no symptom free interval greater than 2 months during that time. Major depressive disorder (as an episode) requires at least 2 weeks of symptoms and can be superimposed (double depression). (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Premorbid depressive personality traits because he says he has never really felt happy and this represents a stable character trait pattern
options.rationale: Depressive personality is not a Diagnostic and Statistical Manual diagnosis; his symptom pattern fits persistent depressive disorder criteria. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Persistent depressive disorder (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision) requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults, with at least 2 of appetite change, sleep change, low energy, low self esteem, poor concentration or hopelessness, and no symptom free interval greater than 2 months. Superimposed major depressive episodes are common (double depression). Treatment combines psychological therapy (cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy) with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Response is often slower than in acute major depressive disorder. Rule out substance use, hypothyroidism and bipolar spectrum disorder first.
key_points: Persistent depressive disorder: depressed mood most days for at least 2 years without a symptom free interval above 2 months.
Superimposed major depressive episodes are common (double depression).
Treatment: cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy plus antidepressant.
explanation.pearls: Depressed mood most days for at least 2 years without a symptom free interval above 2 months in the absence of mania is persistent depressive disorder; treat with cognitive behavioural therapy plus an antidepressant (avoid restarting a previously failed sertraline dose).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual 5th edition Text Revision

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome recognition after olanzapine dose increase in schizophrenia
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 34 year old man with schizophrenia. His olanzapine was increased from 10 to 20 mg 8 days ago for worsening delusions. He now presents with 24 hours of fever, muscle stiffness and confusion. Family report he has been very still for the last 12 hours, sweating and refusing food. He is not aggressive. He has no recent illicit substance use. He has no known allergies. His usual medication is olanzapine 20 mg daily, plus sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for mood stabilisation. He has no cardiac history.

On examination he has generalised lead pipe rigidity, diaphoresis, altered conscious level (Glasgow Coma Score 12), and dysautonomia. Investigations show creatine kinase 8400 U/L (rising), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L (baseline 76), white cell count 14 x10^9/L, urinalysis myoglobin positive. Blood cultures and lumbar puncture have been sent to exclude sepsis and central nervous system infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Diaphoresis, lead pipe rigidity throughout, no clonus, no ocular clonus, Glasgow Coma Score 12, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 8400 U/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, myoglobin positive urine, white cell count 14 x10^9/L, lumbar puncture normal opening pressure and clear fluid pending microscopy, computed tomography head normal

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease olanzapine, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, targeted temperature management, dantrolene if severe rigidity or hyperthermia
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome after antipsychotic dose escalation is treated by immediate cessation of the offending antipsychotic, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to prevent acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis, targeted temperature management with active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation, and dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg intravenously for severe rigidity or hyperthermia. Bromocriptine 2.5 mg 8 hourly oral is an alternative dopamine agonist. Sodium valproate is continued or ceased depending on clinical judgement. Intensive care admission is standard. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 30 mg to treat presumed catatonia and to add lorazepam 2 mg intravenously as a bridging step for the catatonia
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is precipitated by antipsychotic dose escalation and requires immediate cessation of the offending antipsychotic; increasing it is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

options.text: Cease olanzapine and give cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as a targeted serotonin blockade strategy for the presumed serotonin toxicity
options.rationale: Cyproheptadine is used for serotonin syndrome; the clinical picture (lead pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, hyperthermia) fits neuroleptic malignant syndrome rather than serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation). (Source: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

options.text: Continue olanzapine at current dose, give oral paracetamol 1 g and admit for observation with 4 hourly vital signs on the psychiatric ward
options.rationale: Delayed intensive care management with a raised creatine kinase and hyperthermia risks rhabdomyolysis and death; immediate cessation of antipsychotic and intensive supportive management is required. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

options.text: Give haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular as rapid tranquillisation for the agitation because he has established schizophrenia diagnosis history
options.rationale: Adding a second antipsychotic is contraindicated in neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines are used for agitation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life threatening reaction to antipsychotic exposure, typically within 2 weeks of initiation or dose escalation. Diagnosis rests on the tetrad of hyperthermia, lead pipe rigidity, altered mental state and dysautonomia, with markedly raised creatine kinase and often rhabdomyolysis. Treatment is immediate cessation of the offending antipsychotic, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation, and dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg intravenously or bromocriptine 2.5 mg 8 hourly oral in severe cases; intensive care admission is standard. Serotonin syndrome is distinguished by clonus, hyperreflexia and recent serotonergic exposure. Rechallenge with a different antipsychotic at low dose after full recovery of at least 2 weeks is possible under specialist supervision.
key_points: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: hyperthermia, lead pipe rigidity, altered mental state, dysautonomia, raised creatine kinase.
Treatment: cease antipsychotic, intravenous fluids, active cooling, dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg intravenously in severe cases.
Serotonin syndrome is distinguished by clonus, hyperreflexia and recent serotonergic exposure.
explanation.pearls: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome after olanzapine dose escalation: cease olanzapine immediately, aggressive intravenous fluids, active cooling, dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg intravenously for severe rigidity or hyperthermia, intensive care admission.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Guidance on Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
